title: Uluṟu
summary: Uluṟu is a great sandstone rock in central Australia, part of Uluṟu-Kata Tjuṯa National Park. For Aṉangu, the Yankunytjatjara and Pitjantjatjara people, it was shaped by creation ancestors who left laws in the land, held in Tjukurpa. Aboriginal people have lived in Central Australia for over 30,000 years; Aṉangu were recognised as Traditional Owners in 1985.

uncertainty.note: Parks Australia gives Aboriginal occupation of Central Australia as more than 30,000 years (a minimum, for the region rather than the rock itself). The end year, 1985, marks recognition of Aṉangu as Traditional Owners of the park.

as_recorded.value: Aboriginal people have inhabited Central Australia for more than 30,000 years
In 1985, after more than 35 years of campaigning, Aṉangu were recognised as the Traditional Owners of the park

where.modern_name: Uluṟu, Uluṟu-Kata Tjuṯa National Park, Northern Territory, Australia
where.historical_name: Uluṟu, in the country of the Aṉangu (Yankunytjatjara and Pitjantjatjara); later also called Ayers Rock by Europeans

importance.justification: A World Heritage place of continuing cultural significance to Aṉangu and one of the best-known landmarks in Australia.

reviewer_note: The 30,000-year figure is for Central Australia, not Uluru specifically; Aṉangu significance is paraphrased from Parks Australia and should be reviewed with Aṉangu-authored material.
